Join from

Only selected letters will begin a connecting stroke.

Join to

Only selected letters will receive a connecting stroke.

A join is shown only when both its starting and receiving character are selected and the handwriting style supports that pair. Contextual forms that depend on a join before or after the character return to the base form when that join is not selected. Adjust any preset to make a custom focus set.
When this option is off, joins use the same appearance as the letters. When it is on, only the connecting strokes use these settings.

5Handwriting guides
The Admin-authored position remains the default. On the preview, drag any visible stroke number to make a temporary user adjustment for the current tab. With “apply moved position to all matching characters” enabled, the same character and stroke number move together everywhere in the current preview. The leader starts clear of the number and, when a start-point marker is visible, stops with a visible gap before that marker.
Arrow placement can be authored for each character in the Admin Character Editor. Characters without saved arrow positions use one fallback arrow from the stroke start. Arrow outside offset affects only the direction arrows; stroke numbers have their own independent offset above.
Full height uses cap to descender for every character. Wrap height snaps each character to its actual writing zone — for example d: cap to baseline, a: x-height to baseline, p: x-height to descender. When practice-row boxes are enabled, Wrap off uses repeating full-height boxes; Wrap on copies the trace-row character box pattern so the student can follow the same spacing and letter zones without seeing the letters.

About Handwriting Workbench

Teaching philosophy, purpose and approach

About Handwriting Workbench

Old Terrain, New Skills — New Terrain, Old Skills

Handwriting Workbench has been designed around one central teaching philosophy:

Old terrain, new skills. New terrain, old skills.

In simple terms:

When introducing a new skill, practise it in a familiar situation.

When introducing a new situation, use skills the student already knows.

Learning becomes much more difficult when too many things change at the same time.

If a student is learning a new letter, they should not necessarily also be expected to cope with smaller writing, unfamiliar guidelines, reduced tracing support and a new word all at once.

Likewise, when a student moves into a new type of activity, it can be helpful to use movements, letters or words they already know.

The aim is to introduce challenge while retaining enough familiarity for the student to concentrate on what is actually being learned.

This philosophy is the reason Handwriting Workbench is designed to be so adjustable.

The program does not expect every learner to progress through the same worksheet, at the same size, with the same amount of tracing or at the same speed.

The worksheet should adapt to the learner — the learner should not have to be pushed to fit the worksheet.

Why I Created This Program

Handwriting Workbench was created to give teachers, parents and students a more flexible way to practise handwriting.

Many handwriting resources use a fixed progression: a particular letter size, a set number of tracing repetitions, fixed line spacing and a predetermined point at which students are expected to move from tracing to independent writing.

That approach can work well for some students, but students do not all develop handwriting skills at the same rate or in the same way.

A student may understand letter formation but still need help with pencil control.

Another may have good fine-motor control but need additional support with starting points or stroke direction.

One student may be ready for smaller handwriting while another benefits from continuing to use larger movements.

Some students may need additional tracing before moving to independent practice, while others may need very little.

For this reason, Handwriting Workbench is intended to give the person teaching the student control over how difficult the activity becomes and which parts of the task change.

Building on What the Student Already Knows

The idea of old terrain, new skills — new terrain, old skills can be applied throughout handwriting development.

Old Terrain, New Skill

When introducing something new, keep as much of the surrounding activity familiar as practical.

For example, if a student already knows particular letters confidently, those familiar letters can be used when introducing a new skill such as joining.

The letters are familiar.

The joining movement is new.

Or a student may already be comfortable producing straight lines, curves and circles during pencil-control exercises.

Those familiar movements can then become the foundation for introducing letters that contain similar movements.

The student is learning something new, but they are not starting from nothing.

They are building on movements and knowledge they already have.

New Terrain, Old Skill

The same idea works in the other direction.

Once a skill is familiar, it can be used in a new situation.

A student who can confidently form individual letters might begin using those same letters within short words.

Later, familiar words might be used within phrases or sentences.

The context changes, but the underlying handwriting skills remain familiar.

A progression might therefore look something like:

movement → letter → word → phrase → sentence

At each stage, familiar skills provide a foundation for the next activity.

Avoid Changing Everything at Once

A student can appear to be struggling with handwriting when the real problem is simply that too many demands have changed simultaneously.

Imagine a student who has been successfully tracing large letters with clear starting points and stroke guidance.

The next worksheet introduces:

  • a new letter;
  • smaller handwriting;
  • narrower guidelines;
  • no tracing;
  • no stroke arrows;
  • and an unfamiliar word.

If the student struggles, it becomes difficult to determine what caused the difficulty.

Was the new letter the problem?

Was the writing too small?

Did the student still need tracing?

Were they unsure where to begin?

Was the word unfamiliar?

Or was it simply too much change at one time?

Handwriting Workbench is designed so these elements can be changed independently.

This allows the teacher to introduce one significant challenge while keeping other parts of the activity familiar.

Change One Major Challenge at a Time

A useful principle when using Handwriting Workbench is:

Where practical, change one major learning demand at a time.

For example, instead of moving directly from:

large fully traced letters

to:

small independent sentence writing

progress could occur through a series of smaller steps:

Large traced letters

↓

Large letters with reduced tracing support

↓

Large independent letters

↓

Slightly smaller familiar letters

↓

Familiar letters within words

↓

Words with reduced guidance

↓

Independent words and sentences

This is only an example.

The correct progression will differ between students.

The purpose of Handwriting Workbench is not to decide automatically when a learner should move to the next stage.

The program provides the tools.

The teacher, parent or person working with the student decides how those tools should be used.

Why the Program Is So Adjustable

The large number of options in Handwriting Workbench is intentional.

They are not included simply to provide more settings.

Each setting allows part of the learning task to be adjusted without necessarily changing everything else.

Depending on the activity, users can alter things such as:

  • handwriting style;
  • letter size;
  • guideline spacing;
  • page spacing;
  • tracing support;
  • trace and practice rows;
  • starting points;
  • stroke direction;
  • stroke arrows;
  • stroke numbers;
  • pencil-control exercises;
  • word and sentence content;
  • and the amount of independent practice.

This means two students learning the same letter do not necessarily need the same worksheet.

One student might require a large character with substantial tracing assistance.

Another might practise the same character at a smaller size with only a starting point.

Another may already be using that character independently within words.

The learning objective may be similar, while the amount of support can be completely different.

Pencil Control Before Perfect Letters

Handwriting is not only about remembering what a letter looks like.

A learner also needs to develop control over the movements required to produce it.

For this reason, Handwriting Workbench includes pencil-control activities that can be used before, alongside or independently of letter practice.

These may include movements such as:

  • straight downstrokes;
  • horizontal movements;
  • diagonal movements;
  • clockwise and anticlockwise curves;
  • circles;
  • arches;
  • waves;
  • loops;
  • changes of direction;
  • and repeating movement patterns.

These exercises allow a movement to be practised without also requiring the learner to remember an entire letter.

Once the movement becomes familiar, it can then appear again as part of letter formation.

Again, the principle is:

Old terrain, new skills. New terrain, old skills.

A familiar movement can become part of a new letter.

A familiar letter can then become part of a new word.

A familiar word can become part of a new sentence.

Learning develops by building on what is already secure.

Gradually Reducing Support

Support does not have to disappear in a single step.

A student can move gradually from highly guided practice towards independent handwriting.

For example:

full tracing

can become:

lighter tracing

then:

starting points and stroke guidance

then:

guidelines only

and eventually:

independent writing.

Different forms of assistance can also be removed independently.

A student may no longer need to trace a letter but may still benefit from a starting point.

Another student may remember where to start but still need assistance with stroke direction.

Another may form letters correctly but continue to benefit from larger guidelines while developing consistency.

The ability to change these elements separately allows support to be reduced gradually rather than removed all at once.

Different Students Need Different Pathways

Handwriting Workbench is intended to support individual learning rather than prescribe a single pathway that every student must follow.

This does not mean handwriting instruction should have no structure.

It means the size of each learning step can be adjusted.

Some students may move rapidly from tracing to independent writing.

Others may benefit from considerably more repetition.

A learner may progress quickly with one type of movement but need additional practice with another.

A student who has been working independently may also temporarily require additional support when something new is introduced.

Progress does not always mean making every part of the worksheet harder.

Sometimes progress means introducing just one new challenge while allowing everything else to remain familiar.

Australian Handwriting Styles

Another goal of Handwriting Workbench is to support handwriting approaches used across Australian states and territories without requiring a completely different program for each one.

Australian handwriting styles share many underlying principles, but letter shapes, joins, terminology and teaching conventions can vary.

Where appropriate styles are available, Handwriting Workbench allows users to select the handwriting style relevant to their teaching requirements while continuing to use the same worksheet and practice tools.

The aim is not to create a new handwriting style or replace handwriting guidance provided by education authorities.

The program is intended to provide flexible tools that can be used to practise the styles being taught.

A Tool for Teachers — Not a Replacement for Teachers

Handwriting Workbench does not attempt to determine what every student should learn next.

A computer program does not know the learner in front of it.

Teachers and others working directly with students can observe things software cannot easily understand:

  • hesitation;
  • fatigue;
  • frustration;
  • confidence;
  • pencil grip;
  • movement;
  • consistency;
  • and whether the student is genuinely ready for the next challenge.

For that reason, Handwriting Workbench is deliberately designed as a teaching tool rather than an automated teaching system.

The program provides options that allow the activity to be adjusted.

The person teaching decides which options are appropriate.

Keeping the Program Universal

Handwriting Workbench has deliberately been designed to be useful across a wide range of students, activities and teaching situations.

Rather than producing a collection of fixed worksheets, the aim is to provide a system from which many different worksheets and learning activities can be created.

A teacher might use the program to create:

  • an early pencil-control activity;
  • a single-letter tracing page;
  • a student's name;
  • frequently used words;
  • spelling words;
  • handwriting joins;
  • short phrases;
  • sentence practice;
  • targeted revision;
  • or independent handwriting activities.

The same program can therefore remain useful as the learner progresses.

Instead of searching for a completely different worksheet every time something needs to change, the existing activity can often simply be adjusted.

This is also why the program is intended to be universal rather than built around a single fixed teaching sequence.

It provides the tools needed to meet the learner where they are and adjust the activity as they progress.

Why the Program Is Free

Handwriting Workbench has been developed as a practical educational tool.

My aim is to make it genuinely useful and accessible to teachers, parents and students rather than place basic handwriting practice behind a subscription or require schools to purchase another software package simply to create worksheets.

The program may continue to develop as new features, handwriting styles and teaching tools are added.

Keeping the program freely accessible also makes it easier for teachers to use the same tool with colleagues, students and families without having to consider individual licences before sharing an activity.

Any applicable terms of use, acknowledgements and third-party licensing information are provided separately within the program.

The Goal

The goal of Handwriting Workbench is not to produce the most complicated handwriting worksheet.

It is to make it easy to produce the right worksheet for the student at that point in their learning.

Sometimes that will mean more guidance.

Sometimes it will mean less.

Sometimes it will mean larger movements, additional repetition or returning to pencil-control activities.

Sometimes it will mean giving the learner greater independence.

The important thing is that progression can occur in manageable steps while building on skills the student already has.

Old Terrain, New Skills.

New Terrain, Old Skills.

Teach the new skill using familiar terrain.

Introduce new terrain using familiar skills.

Change the challenge when the learner is ready — not simply because a standard worksheet says it is time.

Privacy

How Handwriting Workbench handles information

Privacy

This program is designed to operate entirely on your device and does not collect, store or transmit personal information.

No account, login or registration is required. Information entered into the program, including names, words, worksheet content and settings, is processed locally within your browser and is not sent to us.

Generated worksheets, PDFs, posters and animations are created on your device. We do not receive or retain copies of the content you create.

The program does not collect student information, handwriting samples, learning results or other educational records.

Because the program operates locally, users remain responsible for the storage, sharing and protection of any files they create.

If this privacy approach changes in the future, this notice will be updated before any new collection of personal information is introduced.

Generate Practice Exercises

Build worksheet content, review it, then send it to the normal Practice Worksheet exercise list.

Language & Literacy
Maths & Numbers

Spelling words

Filter the editable master dictionary by group, difficulty, syllables, part of speech, decodable status, length or letter pattern. You can still paste a teacher-supplied list.

Phonics / spelling-pattern words

Generate from editable phonics, grapheme or sound tags in the master dictionary, with optional length, group, difficulty and syllable filters. Written-pattern tags can be suggested automatically; sound tags such as short-i remain teacher-editable.

Letter patterns

Create repeated handwriting patterns from chosen letters. Useful for practising repeated movements, joins and transitions without needing full words.
Separate letters with spaces or commas. A typed group such as “th” is treated as one unit.

Numbers

Generate individual numbers for numeral formation, place-value practice or copying.

Random maths questions

Generate mixed or single-operation questions randomly from the number ranges you choose. This is intended for varied practice rather than a fixed fact sequence.

Structured maths practice

Build a systematic set around selected facts. For example, selecting 2 and partners 1–12 produces 2 + 1…2 + 12, subtract-2 facts, the 2 times table, or the matching divide-by-2 facts.
Use ranges or individual numbers. The selected number becomes the fact being practised: +2, −2, ×2 or ÷2.

Sight words

Sight-word levels now come from the same master dictionary as spelling and phonics. Levels are editable in Admin and are convenience groupings rather than a claim about a particular curriculum sequence.

Sentence starters

Generate short prompts that can be copied as handwriting practice or completed by the learner.

Generated exercises

One generated item per line. You can edit this list directly before adding it to the worksheet.
0 items
Only this exercise's content is replaced. Its position, row counts and universal/local formatting settings are kept.
